terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to count the year's callouts per hill and group their dates.

tasks.title: Callouts per hill
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `callout_counts.py`, write the line that imports `Counter` from `collections`. Then write a function called `hill_counts` that takes a list of hills, one for each callout, and gives back a `Counter` of how many callouts each hill had. For `hills` it gives back `Counter({'Scarth Fell': 3, 'Lowther Crag': 3, 'Cairn Dubh': 1, 'Garve Edge': 1})`. Print what it gives back for `hills`.

Check calls `hill_counts` with lists of its own, an empty one among them, and looks at the counts it gives back and whether they are a `Counter`.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on counting with Counter.
Write the import line, then the def line.
Count the list with a Counter, and give it back.
Print what hill_counts gives back for hills, and compare it with the log.
hints: A plain dictionary has no key for a hill the first time it comes, so `counts[hill] = counts[hill] + 1` stops there with a `KeyError`.
A `Counter` made from a list counts every item in it by itself, and gives 0 for a key it has not seen.
The shape is `from collections import Counter` above the function, and `return Counter(hills)` inside it.

tasks.title: The busiest hills
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, write a function called `busiest` that takes a list of hills and a number `n`, and gives back a list of the `n` hills with the most callouts, each as a tuple `(hill, count)`: the most first, and hills with the same count in the order they first came in the list. When there are fewer than `n` hills, it gives back all of them. For `hills` and `2` it gives back `[('Scarth Fell', 3), ('Lowther Crag', 3)]`. Print what it gives back for `hills` and `2`.

Check calls `busiest` with lists and numbers of its own, a tie among them, and looks at the list it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on the most common.
Count the hills with a Counter, as in Task 1.
Ask the Counter for the n most common, and print what you get.
hints: A Counter knows which keys have the highest counts, and keeps keys with the same count in the order they first came.
A Counter has a method that gives back a list of its highest counts, each a tuple of the key and its count, the most first, as many as you ask for.

tasks.title: Dates by hill
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, write the line that imports `defaultdict` from `collections`. Then write a function called `dates_by_hill` that takes a log, a list of `(date, hill)` tuples, and gives back a dictionary of each hill and a list of the dates of its callouts, in the order of the log. A `defaultdict` or a plain dictionary may come back. For `year` the dates of `'Cairn Dubh'` are `['02/02/2026']`. Print what it gives back for `year`.

Check calls `dates_by_hill` with logs of its own, an empty one among them, and looks at the dictionary it gives back.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on grouping with defaultdict.
Make a defaultdict whose new keys start as an empty list.
Go through the log, and add each date to the list of its hill.
Give back the dictionary, and print it for year.
hints: Each hill's list must be there before a date can be added to it, and a plain dictionary stops with a `KeyError` on the first date of each hill.

A `defaultdict` is given the kind of value each new key starts with, and makes one the first time a key is asked for. For lists, the kind goes in without round brackets: the defaultdict calls it itself.
The shape is `dates = defaultdict(list)`, then `for date, hill in log:` with `dates[hill].append(date)`, then `return dates`.

tasks.title: How many on one hill
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, write a function called `callouts_on` that takes what `dates_by_hill` gives back, a `defaultdict` of each hill and its dates, and a hill, and gives back how many callouts that hill had: `0` for a hill that is not in it. Leave the dictionary it is given as it was: asking about a hill must not add it. Print what it gives back for `dates_by_hill(year)` and `"Black Knowe"`.

Check calls `callouts_on` with a `defaultdict` of its own and hills that are in it and not, and looks at what it gives back and at whether the dictionary is as it was afterwards.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson on what a defaultdict does when it is asked.
Find out whether the hill is in the dictionary at all.
Give back how many dates it has when it is, and 0 when it is not.
Print the dictionary after a call for a hill that is not in it, and check it did not grow.
hints: A defaultdict makes a missing key the moment you read it with square brackets, even only to look.
Asking whether a key is in a dictionary never makes it, and neither does the dictionary method that takes a value to give back for a missing key.
The shape is `if hill in dates:` with `return len(dates[hill])` under it, then `return 0`.
